doc.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Marimba with Ragland and playing bass drum
summary: Besides duty he studied marimba with a Columbus Symphony percussionist and chose the bass drum for its role in the cadence.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: So anymore about your experience about your duty assignment at this air base

There wasn’t really that much to do. Cause Colonel Davis, he was hard on the trumpet players cause they he wanted them to play readily and retreat and all the rest of the Bugle calls. So the trumpet they had a hard time. But other than it was a learning experience and it was a way that I didn’t learn in school. What I didn’t learn in school I learned in the army. I started to take Marimba lessons from a percussionist in the Columbus Symphony orchestra. Ragland. You ever heard of him?
Oh yeah he was a fantastic percussionist, and a mallet man. So I studied with him for a while.
I’m sorry which symphony was that again?
What other assignments did you have in the military? You were designated a bass drummer but did you actually play all the other instruments?

I played all of the percussion instruments. I played the bass drum because nobody had the will to do it. I was the one that said, “I don’t mind playing the bass drum” because I like to listen to the cadence and the bass drum is essential to the cadence. If you don’t hear that the cadence isn’t being played right and you loose the time, and everyone gets frustrated. So it’s important.
